ra: Elioun/Hypsistos is the primordial high god of the Phoenician theogony in Philo of Byblos.
Phoenician sky-god of the theogony.
Phoenician earth-goddess of the theogony.
Elos, the Phoenician El, is the chief god of Philo's theogony.
Sydyk (Righteousness) is a primordial deity in Philo's theogony.
Misor (Uprightness) is a primordial deity in Philo's theogony.
Chousor the craftsman-god belongs to the Phoenician pantheon per Philo.
Taautos the scribe-god is a deity of Philo's Phoenician theogony.
The Kabeiroi/Dioskouroi, sons of Sydyk, are the Great Gods of the Phoenician seafaring cult in Philo.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.15-16): Ouranos and Ge are children of Elioun/Hypsistos.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.15-16): Ge is daughter of Elioun/Hypsistos.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.16): the sibling pair Ouranos and Ge marry and beget Elos/Kronos and his brothers.
Ouranos and Ge are both children of Elioun, brother and sister as well as consorts in Philo.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.16-21): Elos/Kronos is son of Ouranos and Ge and overthrows his father.
Philo: Elos/Kronos is son of Ge by Ouranos.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.21): Elos/Kronos makes war on, castrates and dethrones his father Ouranos.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.25): the Kabeiroi/Dioskouroi are the sons of Sydyk.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.14): Taautos is the son of Misor.
Philo pairs Sydyk and Misor as a kindred dyad of the same generation (Righteousness and Uprightness).
Philo of Byblos explicitly identifies the Phoenician chief god Elos with the Greek Kronos (interpretatio graeca).
Elos is the Hellenized form of Northwest Semitic El; Philo's Elos corresponds to the Ugaritic/Canaanite high god El.
Philo renders the Phoenician sky-god with the Greek name Ouranos, equating the two (interpretatio graeca).
Philo renders the Phoenician earth-goddess with the Greek name Ge (Gaia), equating the two (interpretatio graeca).
Chousor is the Hellenized form of Ugaritic/Canaanite Kothar-wa-Khasis, the craftsman-god; same divine figure across the corpora.
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.9.24): Taautos is the one whom the Egyptians call Thouth (Thoth), the inventor of writing.
Philo names the sons of Sydyk Kabeiroi, the Phoenician interpretatio of the Greek Cabeiri (Great Gods of Samothrace).
Philo (Praep. Ev. 1.10.25) names the sons of Sydyk Dioskouroi as well as Kabeiroi/Corybantes.
